    Sources indicate that if you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these notable details.

    The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

    According to recent reports, based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

    The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized consumers.

    British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

    The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who at the moment have the card, or those who have received a newly introduced cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

    Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

    Recent findings suggest that the British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

    Industry observers note that the British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:.

    There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

    British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

    In a recent development, there are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:.

    British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

    Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

    Often one of the substantial challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

    This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get the card in a household, etc.

    There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

    Industry observers note that one of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

    Industry observers note that if you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

    If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:.

    There are some basic terms to be aware of:.

    Industry observers note that british Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

    One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

    This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

    With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

    This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

    This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

    That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:.

    There are several Avios currencies, with three belonging to International Airlines Group (IAG) airlines — there’s British Airways, Aer Lingus, and Iberia. There are also two other US-based credit cards that directly earn Avios from these airlines. Specifically, we’re talking about the Iberia Visa Card (learn more) and Aer Lingus Visa Card (learn more).

    Beyond that, the card can be worth having for the discounts offered on both paid tickets (up to 10% off) or award tickets (up to $200 in statement credits), which can cover the annual fee over and over. That noted, the card would be even stronger if it offered a free checked bag and lounge access as benefits — though I’d expect the annual to increase if those were added, especially the latter perk.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    In a recent development, the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    Sources indicate that in a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    According to recent reports, “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver stated in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    Sources indicate that the August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, mentioned that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    According to recent reports, separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

    His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

    This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

    According to recent reports, the Boeing 787 Dreamliner is central to several major airlines’ long-haul fleets, with Rolls-Royce's Trent 1000 serving as one of its two available engine options. However, the relationship between the engine manufacturer and major customers has changed over the years. The biggest fleets are not automatically the biggest believers, as ANA, British Airways and Air Fresh Zealand steer new deliveries toward GE Aerospace’s GEnx.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, LATAM Airlines has returned to the Trent 1000 XE. Examining five 787 operators, namely ANA, Singapore Airlines, British Airways, LATAM and Air New Zealand, reveals how differently airlines are approaching the powerplant behind their Dreamliners. Some are expanding GE-powered fleets, while others are maintaining or renewing their relationship with Rolls-Royce.

    As the world's largest operator of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, according to its own data, All Nippon Airways, based in Japan, maintains a fleet of 90 787s across the 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10 variants. Just over 80 of these aircraft are equipped with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines.

    However, following years of reliability challenges with the Trent 1000, ANA has increasingly turned to GE Aerospace's GEnx engines for its newer 787 deliveries, marking a gradual shift away from Rolls-Royce. In 2019, ANA was significantly affected by blade issues within the Trent 1000 engines powering its fleet.

    According to recent reports, some blades developed cracks, partly due to vibration under certain operating conditions. In some cases, blades separated from the rotor, potentially resulting in engine failure. Additional engine challenges involved corrosion around the blade shanks (the sections attaching the blades to the rotor).

    In a recent development, this corrosion led to cracking and the possibility of blades breaking away during operation. These issues affected ANA's 787s equipped with the Trent 1000 Package B and C engines, forcing groundings and repairs at the time, as noted by KN Aviation. Due to the problems ANA experienced with its Trent engines, the airline committed to equipping its future 787s with General Electric's GEnx engine.

    In a recent development, on February 25, 2025, the manufacturer announced that it would move forward with the GEnx, a proven powerplant that has been in service for more than 15 years. GE states that the engine has accumulated more than 62 million flight hours, with over 3,000 units in service and on order, including spare units. The GEnx also powers two-thirds of all 787 aircraft at the moment in operation.

    Singapore Airlines has the unique distinction of being the first airline to operate the 787-10. According to Options, the airline officially received its first 787-10 on March 25, 2018. The aircraft began its inaugural flight from Boeing's South Carolina plant, located in North Charleston, near Charleston International Airport (CHS). After 22 hours, the aircraft landed in Singapore via Osaka.

    That initial delivery was the first of a planned fleet of 49 Dreamliners. Fast-forward eight years, and according to Planespotters.net, Singapore Airlines currently has 26 of the aircraft in active service and two parked, for a total of 28 787s. Given that each Dreamliner is powered by two Trent 1000 engines, the airline maintains 56 units of the Rolls-Royce powerplant across its current fleet.

    Industry observers note that singapore Airlines primarily introduced the 787-10 for regional and medium-haul operations, with the aircraft configured to accommodate 337 passengers across two classes. The airline initially deployed the Dreamliner on routes to Osaka and Perth, demonstrating its role in serving high-demand regional markets.

    Much like ANA, British Airways operates all three 787 variants: the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10. The airline maintains 12 787-8s, 18 787-9s, and 12 787-10s, giving it a total fleet of 42 Dreamliners, according to company sources. While the Trent 1000 had enjoyed several years as the primary engine of BA's 787 fleet, the London fog began to obscure the partnership two years ago.

    According to recent reports, in 2024, the airline selected GE's GEnx-1B engine for six of its incoming 787s rather than maintain its course with Rolls-Royce and its Trent 1000 engines. At the time, BA CEO and Chairman Sean Doyle told Aviation Week that "we ran a competition this time around, and we factored in cost and quality, your total cost of maintenance, and that's been the driver of our decision.".

    The decision marked a significant shift in British Airways' long-standing relationship with Rolls-Royce, with the airline increasingly turning to the American manufacturer for its future Dreamliner deliveries. In terms of future orders, London South East states that the airline right now has 32 787-10s on order, all of which will be powered by GE engines. This represents a gut punch for Rolls-Royce and signals a significant shift in BA's confidence in the two manufacturers.

    Sources indicate that of this large order, two aircraft have very recently been delivered. One joined the manufacturer on October 14, and another followed closely on November 7. With two of the fresh GE-powered Dreamliners already delivered, British Airways is beginning to put that transition into practice, leaving Rolls-Royce with a shrinking role in the airline's future 787 fleet.

    LATAM has a fleet of around 400 aircraft, as reported by ALN News. Providing a large portion of the airline's passenger capacity is its 787 fleet, which right now consists of 41 aircraft. By 2028, LATAM aims to increase that number to 48, according to its 2026 third-quarter report.

    Like many companies making the switch, in 2023 GE noted that LATAM had decided to equip its next 787 deliveries with GEnx engines. AeroTime reports that the 2023 order consisted of 16 787-9s, with LATAM choosing the GEnx due to long-running challenges with the Trent 1000 Package C engines that equipped a portion of its 787 fleet.

    However, all is not lost regarding Rolls-Royce's foothold in the Latin American market. AeroTime states that the engine manufacturer unveiled that LATAM has once again selected its upgraded Trent 1000 XE engine. The selection provides Rolls-Royce with a customer win that it can point to as it seeks to rebuild confidence in its engines amid concerns among global carriers operating the 787 family.

    Recent findings suggest that the selection also signals a renewed commitment to Rolls-Royce, particularly as LATAM looks to expand its long-haul network and strengthen the efficiency of its existing Dreamliner fleet. Regarding the selection, LATAM CEO Roberto Alvo stated that:.

    “The incorporation of the Trent 1000 XE on our Boeing 787 aircraft supports our efforts to enhance operational efficiency, while providing optionality to capture growth opportunities as we continue developing our long-haul network,”.

    The carrier in this list with the smallest number of 787s is Air Upcoming Zealand, which at the moment operates 14 of the aircraft, with an additional 10 on order, according to the airline's website. Like other airlines operating the 787, the carrier experienced similar troubles with the Trent 1000. In 2019, the organization selected the GEnx engine to power eight of its future 787-10s, with the possibility of increasing that number to 20, according to GE.

    That firm order was valued at more than $480 million (£367 million) at list prices, and deliveries of the GEnx-powered aircraft began in 2022. The Trent 1000 problems had a major impact on the company's operations, with five of its 14 Boeing 787-9s grounded and unavailable at the height of the disruption.

    According to recent reports, the airline described the engine shortage as one of the most significant supply chain challenges facing aviation, and aircraft shortages affected its finances and ability to operate its long-haul network. According to AeroTime, the final stored Dreamliner returned to Auckland (AKL) in June 2026. The aircraft resumed commercial flying two days later, marking an key step toward restoring availability across the carrier's existing widebody fleet.

    The return followed extensive maintenance and engine work. Air Newly introduced Zealand is now getting ready to grow its Dreamliner fleet with a second engine type. Its 10 incoming aircraft comprise five 787-9s and five 787-10s, all powered by GE Aerospace GEnx-1B engines, rather than Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s. Ch-aviation reported that manufacturing delays pushed the first new 787-9 deliveries into 2027.

    Meanwhile, Fleet Wire states two latest aircraft joined the fleet in October 2026. Operating both engine types will require separate spare engines and support arrangements, adding another consideration as the airline expands its Dreamliner operations, including services to Houston, Vancouver, Shanghai and Taipei as aircraft arrive across its network.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways declared it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement.
    • Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.
    • In a recent development, earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways declared it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

    Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

    In a recent development, earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:.

    The Tech giant’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

    According to recent reports, to state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the organization was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

    According to recent reports, norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

    Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,….

    So while the firm hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

    The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline debuted in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

    That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

    But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline enhancement its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

    Recent findings suggest that the company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

    Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “fresh” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

    Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

    I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

    Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

    This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

    Financial challenges at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

    Sources indicate that I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

    What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

While European bankruptcy laws are usually not as generous for restructuring as Chapter 11 in the US, they usually do require the bankruptcy administrator to safe money if this can be done by continuing (partial) operation.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities.
    • At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.
    • Sources indicate that the 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes….

    At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

    Sources indicate that the 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

    However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

    Sources indicate that 🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf.

    WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m.

    Industry observers note that fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

    Industry observers note that footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v.

    This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

    🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。….

    It has been revealed that of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

    We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

    First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

    In a recent development, JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1.

    A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data highlights just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

    🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97.

    Industry observers note that it’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”.

    A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP.

    #157237. Breaking: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    Breaking: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    Recent findings suggest that the power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    Sources indicate that it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller stated that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller stated that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller mentioned.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide remarked.

    King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    According to recent reports, the relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling noted.

    Sources indicate that the bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    #157234. Tech Report: Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1806 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency.
    • Sources indicate that in this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically.
    • Recent findings suggest that for those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

    Sources indicate that in this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

    Recent findings suggest that for those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

    Industry observers note that the exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

    In a recent development, you do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

    It has been revealed that over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

    Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

    Global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

    In a recent development, if you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

    Industry observers note that generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

    According to recent reports, you can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership right now expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

    It has been revealed that you won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

    Sources indicate that there is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

    If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

    Recent findings suggest that it costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

    When you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:.

    While only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

    It has been revealed that on November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

    Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a upcoming Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

    Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

    There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

    Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

    This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

    You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

    The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to enhancement your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

    At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

    To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

    When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

    I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

    As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Air travelers returning home from Thanksgiving can breathe a sigh of relief.

    • And Mother Nature appeared not to have any more major curveballs to throw at travelers between now and Sunday, normally one of the busiest air travel periods of the year as holiday-goers return home.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Air travelers returning home from Thanksgiving can breathe a sigh of relief.

    Flight schedules were close to normal on Friday after a series of storms snarled flights on both coasts during the run-up to Thanksgiving.

    And Mother Nature appeared not to have any more major curveballs to throw at travelers between now and Sunday, normally one of the busiest air travel periods of the year as holiday-goers return home.

    Sources indicate that that came after more than 460 flights were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightAware. The bad weather complicated the plans of tens of thousands of travelers with flights on Thanksgiving Day. East Coast airports serving the metro areas of Fresh York City, Washington, D.C., Boston, Philadelphia and Baltimore were the hardest hit, but disruptions rippled across airports in Florida, the Midwest and the West Coast.

    The main culprit: A Thanksgiving Day coastal storm on the East Coast that was strong enough to cause the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Midtown Manhattan.

    Industry observers note that this week's flight problems came after a chaotic few weeks for air travel in the U.S., which featured a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 — and then tech outages at two of the largest U.S. carriers.

    Now, Mother Nature has interfered with holiday travelers' intends.

    “The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen had told TPG entering the Thanksgiving rush.

    We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

    Major airlines rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions:.

    While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself typically brings much smaller crowds to airports.

    Industry observers note that according to preliminary data from the Transportation Security Administration, Thursday was the single quietest day at U.S. airports in nearly five years.

    According to recent reports, the forecast looks favorable through Sunday as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

    Sources indicate that last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

    According to recent reports, entering the holiday rush, the TSA had projected more than 3 million passengers could fly on Nov. 29. That would be the first time U.S. passenger traffic would eclipse that mark in 2026.

    Here are some things you should do if you've been affected by bad weather this holiday week, or blueprint to fly on the upcoming busy Sunday.

    Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories (see above) that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

    Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

    Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

    According to recent reports, have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:.

    Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

    When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

    However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

    Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

    Just be sure to keep all your receipts.

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the upcoming year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the upcoming year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” remarked Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    Sources indicate that “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Folding fresh language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the matter while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    According to recent reports, colorado Rep. Jason Crow noted moving forward swiftly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    It has been revealed that “I want to pursue a parallel track,” stated Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly remarked the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Industry observers note that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he stated at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying fresh stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    Recent findings suggest that rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., noted she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she stated of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    It has been revealed that that measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    According to recent reports, “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal remarked. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a latest stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    “My district, Latest York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and reveals right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander stated.

    Recent findings suggest that while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any fresh bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    It has been revealed that “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    It has been revealed that that proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    • Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card.

    • Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

    Sources indicate that in this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

    Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

    To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

    The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:.

    Recent findings suggest that the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:.

    If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

    According to recent reports, the first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

    If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

    Industry observers note that the annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

    Industry observers note that the math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

    With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

    Recent findings suggest that so my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a big spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

    Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

    That being remarked, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

    What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

    #157227. The Engineering Tricks Boeing Had To Come Up With To Fit Bigger Fans Under A 1960s Wing

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1831 w)

    The Engineering Tricks Boeing Had To Come Up With To Fit Bigger Fans Under A 1960s Wing

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • During the 1960s, Boeing introduced several aircraft that would transform commercial aviation, including the 727, 737, and 747.
    • According to recent reports, the original 737 was designed around relatively small, narrow engines.
    • Industry observers note that the 1960s marked a period of significant expansion for Boeing, with the manufacturer introducing several aircraft that would transform commercial aviation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    During the 1960s, Boeing introduced several aircraft that would transform commercial aviation, including the 727, 737, and 747. The Boeing 737, which made its first flight in April 1967, was designed for short-haul operations and would eventually become one of the best-selling commercial aircraft families in aviation history.

    According to recent reports, the original 737 was designed around relatively small, narrow engines. However, as engine technology advanced, Boeing faced the challenge of fitting increasingly larger and more efficient engines beneath wings positioned unusually close to the ground. Rather than addressing this limitation through a single redesign, Boeing introduced a series of engineering modifications across successive 737 generations, culminating in the 737 MAX. So, what changes did Boeing make to accommodate these larger engines, and what compromises did they involve?

    Industry observers note that the 1960s marked a period of significant expansion for Boeing, with the manufacturer introducing several aircraft that would transform commercial aviation. After introducing the four-engine Boeing 707 in 1958 and the three-engine 727 in 1962, Boeing developed the twin-engine 737 to serve the growing short-haul market. The first 737 took flight on April 9, 1967, seating approximately 100 passengers and offering a range of around 2,500 miles (4,023 km).

    The original 737 was designed to operate efficiently at airports with limited ground-handling infrastructure. One of the most significant decisions during its development was Boeing engineer Joseph Sutter's proposal to mount the engines beneath the wings rather than on the rear fuselage, as seen on competing aircraft. This arrangement helped define the 737's distinctive design, while its low fuselage allowed ground crews to access baggage compartments and service the aircraft without specialized lifting equipment. This configuration was well suited to the relatively narrow Pratt & Whitney JT8D engines. However, as engine technology advanced, manufacturers increasingly adopted high-bypass turbofans, which improve propulsive efficiency by moving larger volumes of air around the engine core. Their larger fans, however, require considerably more space beneath the wing.

    In a recent development, this became a challenge when Boeing developed the 737 Classic family, beginning with the 737-300. The manufacturer selected the larger CFM56-3 high-bypass turbofan to replace the original JT8D engines, but the aircraft's low wing position and short landing gear left insufficient space for a conventional installation. Boeing therefore had to find a way to accommodate the larger engines while maintaining adequate ground clearance.

    Sources indicate that by the early 1980s, advances in engine technology prompted Boeing to select the CFM56-3 for its latest 737 Classic family, replacing the original low-bypass Pratt & Whitney JT8D with a larger, more fuel-efficient high-bypass turbofan. The engine's fan diameter increased from approximately 40 inches (102 cm) to 60 inches (152 cm), while the aircraft retained its original low-slung architecture. The CFM56-3 offered improved fuel efficiency and lower noise levels, with fuel consumption improvements of approximately 20% compared with the JT8D. However, its larger diameter meant Boeing could not simply replace the existing engines without modifying their installation.

    According to recent reports, working with CFM International, Boeing adapted the CFM56-3 to fit beneath the 737 Classic's low wings. The engine nacelle (the outer casing surrounding the engine) received a distinctive flattened lower profile to maintain sufficient ground clearance. To achieve this, components such as the accessory gearbox were relocated from beneath the engine to its sides. The resulting shape, sometimes nicknamed the "hamster pouch," became one of the 737 Classic's most recognizable features. This engineering compromise allowed Boeing to accommodate the larger engine without undertaking an extensive redesign of the aircraft's landing gear and basic airframe architecture. The table below illustrates the timeline of engine installations across successive Boeing 737 generations, which will be explored throughout this article. For a closer look at the CFM56-3's design, Laura Laster provides a detailed explanation in A Boeing 737 Engine CFM56-3 Quick Overview.

    First Aircraft Fitted (Roll-out).

    Flattened nacelle and relocated accessories.

    Refined nacelle and forward mounting.

    Larger engine with further installation changes.

    However, modifying the nacelle's shape alone was not enough to overcome the 737's ground clearance limitations. Boeing also had to reconsider how the engines were positioned relative to the wings, introducing another engineering solution that would continue to evolve across subsequent generations.

    Industry observers note that nearly a decade after introducing the 737 Classic, Boeing launched the 737 Next Generation (NG) program in November 1993. Designed to compete directly with the Airbus A320 family, the NG represented one of the most extensive upgrades to the 737, introducing a redesigned wing, strengthened landing gear, and improved performance while retaining the aircraft's basic architecture. The new wing featured a greater span of approximately 117 feet, 5 inches (35.79 meters), increased fuel capacity, and improved aerodynamic efficiency, helping extend the aircraft's range and raise its operating ceiling to 41,000 feet (12,497 meters).

    The 737 NG also introduced the CFM56-7B engine, featuring a fan diameter of approximately 61 inches (155 cm), slightly larger than the Classic's CFM56-3. To accommodate larger engines beneath the 737's lower wings, Boeing continued refining an approach first introduced with the Classic: mounting the engines farther forward and higher relative to the wing. This positioned the fan section ahead of the wing's leading edge rather than directly underneath it, helping maintain sufficient ground clearance. The CFM56-7B also delivered approximately 7% better fuel efficiency than its predecessor, along with improved climb performance and reduced noise levels.

    Sources indicate that however, the next generation of high-bypass turbofans required even larger fans to achieve further efficiency improvements. When Boeing began developing the 737 MAX, the aircraft's low wing position and relatively short landing gear once again limited the size of the engines it could accommodate. With the new CFM LEAP engine offering a substantial increase in fan diameter, Boeing faced another challenge: how could it install a larger, more efficient engine without fundamentally redesigning the 737?

    Fast-forward to 2011, when Boeing launched the 737 MAX program as the successor to the 737 Next Generation family. The newly introduced aircraft would be powered exclusively by the CFM International LEAP-1B, a next-generation high-bypass turbofan developed to deliver greater fuel efficiency and lower emissions. The LEAP family introduced several advanced technologies, including 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan blades and improved thermal efficiency. According to CFM International, the engines deliver approximately 15% lower fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation engines. However, Boeing's decision to retain the 737's low-slung architecture meant that the LEAP-1B had to be adapted to fit the aircraft's limited ground clearance.

    According to recent reports, unlike the LEAP-1A, which powers the Airbus A320neo and features a 78-inch (198 cm) fan, the 737 MAX's LEAP-1B was designed with a smaller fan measuring approximately 69.4 inches (176 cm) in diameter. This nearly nine-inch (23 cm) difference was largely driven by the 737's shorter landing gear and lower wing position. The smaller fan also contributed to a lower bypass ratio of approximately 9:1, compared with around 11:1 for the LEAP-1A. Although a higher bypass ratio can improve propulsive efficiency, the LEAP-1B's design allowed Boeing to benefit from newer engine technology without fundamentally redesigning the 737's airframe.

    Despite the smaller fan, the LEAP-1B was still considerably larger than the CFM56-7B used on the 737 NG, which had a fan diameter of approximately 61 inches (155 cm). The increase of more than eight inches (20 cm) meant that reducing the LEAP's fan diameter alone was insufficient to solve the aircraft's ground clearance limitations. Boeing therefore needed to introduce further modifications to the 737 MAX's engine installation and landing gear, raising another question: how could the manufacturer accommodate the larger engines while preserving the aircraft's existing design?

    In a recent development, the Boeing 737 MAX was designed exclusively around the CFM International LEAP-1B engine, allowing Boeing to focus on integrating a single engine type into the existing 737 architecture. However, even with its smaller fan diameter, the LEAP-1B required additional ground clearance. To accommodate the larger engines, Boeing extended the MAX's nose landing gear by approximately eight inches (20 cm), raising the front of the aircraft. This modification was possible because the nose landing gear bay offered more vertical space than the main landing gear bays, making it a more practical solution than substantially redesigning the aircraft's undercarriage.

    Boeing also repositioned the LEAP-1B engines farther forward and higher relative to the wing than on the 737 NG. Combined with the longer nose landing gear and a revised nacelle design, these modifications provided sufficient ground clearance while preserving much of the 737's original architecture. However, the larger, repositioned engines also affected the aircraft's aerodynamic characteristics, particularly at elevated angles of attack. To address differences in handling characteristics, Boeing introduced the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), designed to automatically command nose-down stabilizer trim under certain flight conditions.

    Although these modifications helped Boeing develop a more fuel-efficient competitor to the Airbus A320neo while maintaining commonality with earlier 737 models, the MCAS system subsequently became central to one of the most serious crises in Boeing's history. Investigations into the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019, which killed a combined 346 people, identified serious flaws in pilot training. The accidents ultimately led to the worldwide grounding of the 737 MAX and extensive changes to its flight control systems.

    Boeing's decision to retain the 737's basic architecture allowed it to introduce more efficient engines without developing an entirely new aircraft. However, the design required several compromises, including the LEAP-1B's smaller fan, revised engine mounting, and landing gear modifications. While these changes helped Boeing remain competitive with the Airbus A320neo, the long-term consequences of adapting an aircraft originally designed in the 1960s have proved far more difficult to quantify.

    The financial and reputational costs of the 737 MAX crisis have extended well beyond the aircraft itself. The two fatal accidents, subsequent worldwide grounding, compensation payments, legal proceedings, and production disruptions have cost Boeing tens of billions of dollars. The crisis also intensified scrutiny of Boeing's engineering and certification practices, contributing to a more demanding regulatory environment. The 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 have faced prolonged certification delays, while the separate 777X program has also experienced years of setbacks and extensive regulatory oversight. Meanwhile, Airbus has strengthened its position in the commercial aircraft market, increasing the competitive pressure on Boeing.

    Developing an entirely newly introduced aircraft rather than continuing to modify the 737 might appear to have been a better long-term decision. However, the challenges extend beyond the MAX. Future improvements in propulsion technology could require significantly larger fans or entirely different engine architectures, potentially exceeding the limits of the 737's existing configuration. CFM International's Revolutionary Innovation for Sustainable Engines (RISE) program, for example, is developing open-fan technology targeting the next generation of commercial aircraft, with the potential for substantial fuel-efficiency improvements. As Boeing looks to its next generation of narrowbody aircraft, will further modifications suffice, or is an entirely new design necessary?
