    #157226. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2048 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).
    • I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product.
    • Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

    I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

    Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge challenges. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

    Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

    Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

    10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

    Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

    It has been revealed that we arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is at the moment closed, so we had no lounge option there.

    In a recent development, I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

    In a recent development, boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

    According to recent reports, we boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

    Industry observers note that royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

    These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

    It has been revealed that the tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

    There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

    On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

    There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

    Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

    While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

    Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

    In a recent development, so the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an concern. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

    In a recent development, during boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

    One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

    Industry observers note that airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

    Recent findings suggest that at 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

    The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

    It was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

    The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

    After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

    A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

    The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

    For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

    It has been revealed that just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

    There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

    Sources indicate that the lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

    Recent findings suggest that the primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

    Industry observers note that at 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

    The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

    We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

    From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

    On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

    As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

    It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

    In a recent development, I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

    It has been revealed that to be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

    What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

    At the Races: The newly introduced Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    In a recent development, “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    Sources indicate that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews stated, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” remarked Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    According to recent reports, “I respect them,” he noted. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” mentioned California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, declared he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    In a recent development, they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” noted Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    Recent findings suggest that RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    It has been revealed that thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg introduced Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    According to recent reports, new leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    According to recent reports, investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, confirmed a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    Recent findings suggest that the  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: Upcoming York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who indicates she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the Latest York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    In a recent development, machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly remarked he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the spirit of trying out new ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.
    • According to recent reports, I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could.
    • After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the spirit of trying out new ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

    According to recent reports, I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

    After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉.

    Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

    Industry observers note that on this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That mentioned, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is currently undergoing some refurbishments.

    Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

    Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

    Industry observers note that speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall K, on a previous trip. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge fresh flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

    I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

    Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

    If you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding….

    According to recent reports, thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

    The legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My blueprint was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

    In a recent development, of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

    I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

    No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

    Industry observers note that of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

    Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

    I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

    I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

    Sources indicate that for those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

    I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

    Despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical glitch, so I didn’t take any pictures.

    Industry observers note that I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

    Recent findings suggest that I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

    According to recent reports, neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

    Air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

    I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

    The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

    I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

    Industry observers note that as for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no glitch.

    Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

    One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting newly introduced people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

    Sources indicate that if I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

    Over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

    After being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

    Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

    When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?

    Is Lufthansa Really Hiring 1,000 Pilots By 2033 While Cutting 1,000 Hub Jobs?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that lufthansa has made headlines in recent weeks for multiple potential moves that would impact its workforce.
    • Each respective proposal involves reducing or adding the same number of staff members as the other.
    • On paper, yes, Lufthansa has suggested both cutting 1,000 jobs and hiring 1,000 pilots.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa has made headlines in recent weeks for multiple potential moves that would impact its workforce. On the one hand, proposed cuts could eat into its workforce at its two key hubs, Frankfurt Main Airport (FRA) and Munich Airport (MUC). On the other, an offer has been tabled that would guarantee newly introduced pilot hires ahead if accepted.

    Each respective proposal involves reducing or adding the same number of staff members as the other. It would appear, therefore, that Lufthansa — Europe’s largest airline by fleet count — is heading toward two fairly drastic efforts that would see one area slimmed down for the other to be bolstered by equal measure. The reality is far more complex, though. While there is a sense of irony behind the overall thinking, each decision stems from an entirely isolated issue the carrier is navigating today. So, what is really happening?

    On paper, yes, Lufthansa has suggested both cutting 1,000 jobs and hiring 1,000 pilots. Proposals put forward by Lufthansa to employees internally include the cuts, as reported initially around November 19. In contrast, proposals made to pilot union Vereinigung Cockpit and detailed by Lufthansa just a few days earlier on November 17 would see the airline commit to recruiting the pilots over the coming years.

    According to recent reports, the thinking behind each decision is not so straightforward, however. Cuts appear to have been tabled on the back of Lufthansa’s own deteriorating financial performance. In contrast, Lufthansa offering to hire new pilots looks to be an attempt to break a stalemate with the union that has followed months of talks. As such, the two are not necessarily completely interlinked.

    Nonetheless, were both to materialize, it would indeed leave the airline in a position where it is reducing its workforce in one area, while bolstering it in another. It is unclear whether either will in fact materialize, with Lufthansa telling Simple Flying it had “nothing to add to these media reports” when approached for comment. What is clear is that this year has been tough on carriers, and heated union negotiations have added another headache in Lufthansa’s case.

    According to recent reports, the reasoning given behind the cuts is a worsening financial performance presently, not least due to rising fuel prices. In the letter to employees, obtained by the German Press Agency and reported on by various outlets, the airline’s board clearly laid out its intentions.

    “At the Frankfurt and Munich hubs, we are planning to cut a total of 1,000 full-time positions within the Lufthansa Airlines subgroup,” the letter — signed by chief executive Jens Ritter among others — said. “Lufthansa Airlines is right now not competitive [and] we have reached a point where we need to make even more far-reaching changes,” it added.

    Lufthansa Group financial highlights covering nine months to September 30:.

    The group’s latest financial results, released on November 3, backed up the bleak diagnosis. Stronger revenue and income during the first nine months of the year were clouded by higher operating expenses. Notably, fuel costs rocketed 21% to €6.7 billion ($7.4 billion), despite hedging and reduced consumption, including as flight and passenger numbers fell by 4% and 1%, respectively. As for subsidiary Lufthansa Airlines — where cuts are planned — an adjusted pre-tax loss of €180 million ($198 million) was recorded, against a profit of €147 million ($162 million) a year prior.

    Industry observers note that so, simply put, Lufthansa has found itself grappling with a deteriorating underlying performance at a group level, with its flagship business slipping into the red. It is in this context that staff reductions within the latter were floated to employees. But unfortunately for the carrier, that makes up just one of the areas where pressure has been building.

    The years-long dispute with Vereinigung Cockpit — which initially related to pension scheme changes dating back to 2017, but has since evolved to cover the likes of job progression and security — has only added to its woes. Owing to the deadlock between the two, the union called pilot strikes at the carrier in February, March, and April. Subsequent second-quarter results from Lufthansa detailed that the industrial action had cost it at least €150 million ($165 million), and that six days' worth of strikes in April knocked capacity down 3%. Despite work towards a resolution since, talks between Vereinigung Cockpit and Lufthansa have collapsed recently.

    Key dates from a packed November of Lufthansa-related news:.

    Third-quarter figures show worsening underlying performance at Lufthansa.

    Period of mediation between Lufthansa and Vereinigung Cockpit ends.

    Vereinigung Cockpit “prepared to begin working on the details of proposal”.

    Lufthansa publishes counteroffer instead, including promise of up to 1,000 cockpit hires.

    Vereinigung Cockpit also signals obligation to refrain from strikes has expired.

    Reports emerge Lufthansa planning 1,000 job cuts at key hubs.

    Vereinigung Cockpit-imposed deadline for Lufthansa to return to talks passes.

    Industry observers note that vereinigung Cockpit slams Lufthansa in a statement. No strikes announced.

    A period of arbitration was followed by one of mediation that ended in mid-November, at which point a deal emerged that the union backed but the airline did not. Lufthansa instead tabled a counteroffer, which it mentioned was based on arbitrators’ recommendations and included the proposal of 1,000 newly introduced cockpit hires. Vereinigung Cockpit responded in turn by setting a deadline of November 23 for the airline to withdraw it and return to the negotiating table, which then passed to no avail. That left the union to slam the airline the day after, when it wrote: “Seven months of exploratory talks, three rounds of conciliation, and a total of 18 rounds of discussions with the mediator have apparently been in vain.”.

    Whether the prospect of job cuts was raised because negotiations were reaching a tipping point has been questioned by Vereinigung Cockpit. “Coincidence? Hardly,” it noted in response to reports of the cuts, “what is being built up here is primarily a lot of threatening talk”. That noted, it is no secret that the wider aviation industry has faced struggles this year.

    Industry observers note that KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, another European carrier, said in early November it would look to reduce its workforce by 15% in response to an “increasingly complex” operational environment. Shortly after, Australia’s Qantas signaled it would be cutting 850 corporate roles and outsourcing the work overseas.

    Such measures are being taken in each case against the backdrop of a sustained increase in fuel prices since the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. To put that into perspective, the price of jet fuel averaged 71.9% more over the week to November 20 than it did in the same period a year before, per the International Air Transport Association. Needless to say, ballooning costs have been an glitch for airlines globally of late.

    Unsurprisingly, Lufthansa did refer to such cost pressures upon telling staff of the cuts, writing: “The price of fuel exposes and exacerbates [...] structural weaknesses.” As with its offer to Vereinigung Cockpit, though, there are several questions over what actually comes next.

    Industry observers note that november’s third-quarter figures detailed that Lufthansa Airlines had 39,622 employees as of the end of September, meaning a reduction of 1,000 positions would mark a 2.5% cut to its workforce. Though stark, the results also demonstrated there had been a 0.9% drop — equivalent to 341 employees — in headcount at the subsidiary since a year earlier. Aside from impacting “full-time positions,” Lufthansa has yet to detail how the roles will be axed, which will be affected, and over what timeline. Companies can avoid directly slashing jobs more gradually through attrition, for instance, a tool KLM said it was to use. Another thing to flag is Lufthansa’s announcement last year that 4,000 administrative positions were to go, and so whether the latest round of cuts would be linked to these remains to be seen.

    Industry observers note that as for its offer to create newly introduced cockpit positions, the headline figure of 1,000 new pilot hires arguably implies a more drastic expansion on Lufthansa's part than would actually materialize. The promised recruitment drive runs through 2033, giving the airline several years to fill the positions. However, previous figures from pilots' union Vereinigung Cockpit, cited by Aviation Direct, point to hundreds of age-related departures over the same period. Around 300 retirements are anticipated in 2026 and 2027 alone, with a further 740 expected between 2029 and 2034. Note that these cover both Lufthansa Classic — where the additions would be made — and Lufthansa Cargo. Either way, they suggest much of the recruitment could simply be needed anyway to replace departing personnel.

    It has been revealed that that could be by design, of course, with Lufthansa’s cost-saving efforts potentially set to go as far as reducing its mainline narrowbody fleet in favor of buoying long-haul operations. Ultimately, though, time will tell what comes next.

    Indeed, Lufthansa has told staff 1,000 positions are to go. It has also floated the idea of committing to hiring 1,000 pilots in the coming years. Details of the former remain few and far between, however. The latter, meanwhile, has by no means been met with enthusiasm from the union it was designed to win over.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that there’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

    So that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

    Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.

    I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir.

    Industry observers note that I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w.

    In a recent development, I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

    Recent findings suggest that I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”.

    I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

    All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

    He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their manufacturer.”.

    Sources indicate that @AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR.

    @AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their company @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL.

    He then attacked American’s rebooking lines at Miami Airport. Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

    Recent findings suggest that @AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1.

    He also has an concern with bathrooms at Miami Airport, which I get, but goodness, he’s repetitive.

    Why do you have the most disgusting bathrooms @iflymia.

    Why are your bathroom so nasty @iflymia.

    Why are your bathroom never clean@iflymia.

    Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia.

    You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia.

    Industry observers note that he then suggested that he’ll fly Delta or United next time, because they can get you where you’re supposed to go. Yeah, sure bro, they’ll get you out of Miami Airport when it’s closed due to an accident.

    It has been revealed that next time I'll fly @united or @Delta because they can actually get you where you are supposed to be when you are supposed to be there…and paid for…unlike the incompetent airline @AmericanAir. I bet your life is full of incompetence.

    He’s also asking Secretary Duffy to investigate American, because “they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America.” We know the Trump administration loves to investigate corruption, I’m sure they’ll get right on that!

    Can you investigate @AmericanAir they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America.

    Honestly, I think American is perfectly justified in banning this guy. He’s violating the organization’s policy on photographing employees, and this kind of behavior doesn’t need to be tolerated.

    Recent findings suggest that it sucks when things go wrong while flying, especially for travel around the holidays. But there’s a fine line between a reasonable complaint, and one that’s completely uncalled for. Posting pictures of random pilots and suggesting they’re the reason you can’t see your family for Thanksgiving is not acceptable.

    What’s even worse is when people explain that crew rest requirements are federally mandated, but you just remain in denial over that, and double down. American, please do everyone else a favor and ban this guy.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in.
    • I’d like to talk about what the fresh password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.
    • Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in. Kimpton generally has this promotion a couple of times per year — we last saw this in summer, and there’s now a newly introduced password for winter.

    I’d like to talk about what the fresh password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.

    Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands. One of those things is the social password. The idea is that seasonally, Kimpton provides a phrase through social media that you’re supposed to say when you check-in, and if you do that, you’ll receive something extra.

    According to recent reports, the new Kimpton password is “this calls for something,” and it’s valid for stays between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027. So just say that when you check-in at a Kimpton property during the promotion period, and you’ll receive a surprise.

    Industry observers note that for those curious about what happens when you say the Kimpton password, I stayed at the Kimpton EPIC Miami some time back, which was my first Kimpton stay in quite a while (and I haven’t stayed at one since either). It was a good value as well, as I was able to use a free night award earned with the New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more).

    It has been revealed that I was curious what the benefit would be for using the password. So I shared the password with the front desk agent. At the conclusion of the check-in experience, he brought out a game show-style wheel. I might have spun too hard, as it must have gone around for about 30 seconds. Go figure I landed on the tile that just had me spin again.

    Sources indicate that then I spun again, and the prize was free parking. I had a car and was staying for two nights, and parking costs $44 per night. So using the Kimpton password saved me nearly $100 — score!!

    Based on looking at the wheel, it seems that some of the other prizes include a free welcome drink, free breakfast, free snacks, and a free movie. There were also a few empty squares, where I guess you don’t win anything. And I’m not sure what the alarm clock, car tipping over, or postcard of Miami get you. Regardless, I’d say those are some awesome prizes, and I got a great reward.

    It’s cute how the Kimpton EPIC Miami makes a game of this. I know there’s a lot of inconsistency when it comes to this benefit across Kimpton properties. Some hotels provide meaningful perks (an upgrade, free, parking, etc.), like I got here, while other hotels provide a 19 cent branded koozie.

    According to recent reports, it’s great that this has stuck around, given that it has presumably become increasingly popular. Years ago not everyone was on social media, so it was a good way to encourage people to follow Kimpton on X, Facebook, Instagram, etc. With the way the internet has evolved, times have changed a bit.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m sure I’m not the only one who finds the concept of saying a password at check-in to be kind of weird. So I think it’s fun to compare notes about how people share the password at the front desk. I find it awkward to just blurt out the password out of nowhere.

    So when I used this for my stay, I noted “I guess I’m supposed to say [social password] as the social password?” That did the trick, but I’d be curious to hear how other Kimpton regulars go about this!

    Between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027, Kimpton’s social password is “this calls for something.” Just state that phrase when you check-in at a Kimpton, and you should get some sort of a surprise. The gift will vary by property, so there’s no reason not to take advantage of this if staying at a Kimpton.

    The last time I used the password I got to spin a wheel at check-in, and then I ended up getting free parking, which was a value of $44 per night.

    If you’ve used the Kimpton password, what was your experience like?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., stated earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    It has been revealed that “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., mentioned during the meeting.

    When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    It has been revealed that “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” noted panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she remarked in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack noted that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    Recent findings suggest that “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack noted in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he said at Thursday’s meeting.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to “What’s in My Bag,” a upcoming series where TPG staffers open their carry-ons, personal items and dopp kits to share the travel essentials they never leave home without. First up: The Points Guy founder, Brian Kelly.

    As a travel expert who’s constantly on the go, I will say some of my favorite things that you’ll find in my bag revolve around staying organized and being comfortable — I always know where my essentials are. At this stage of my life, I’m willing to splurge a bit on handcrafted or well-made products that last. Quality is nonnegotiable.

    It has been revealed that this travel pouch is so chic, but definitely a splurge. It’s made with Saffiano leather and Re-Nylon, an innovative fabric that’s produced from recycled plastic recovered from the ocean. You can find it at Saks Fifth Avenue. I love it for keeping everything I might need on the go organized — with two top zipper pockets and one each on the front and back, I never run out of room.

    Buy: Prada Re-Nylon and Saffiano leather travel pouch, $1,120.

    It has been revealed that these Bose noise-canceling headphones are comfortable and seamlessly connect via Bluetooth. Plus, they are stylish and have great sound quality. The surround sound is awesome.

    Buy: Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones, from $349 (normally $449).

    Sources indicate that as a content creator, I needed a good lav microphone with an iPhone receiver for when I’m out and about. The Rode wireless mic is super easy to use, holds a charge all day and slips right into my travel pouch.

    Buy: Rode ultra-compact wireless microphone system with USB-C connector, $89 (normally $99).

    According to recent reports, my go-to quick snack is Quest protein peanut butter cups — indulgent yet packed with protein. I keep Grüns gummies in my bag for a healthy mix of essential vitamins and prebiotics. They keep me feeling energized and are more than just a multivitamin — they’re made with whole fruits and veggies too.

    Buy: Grüns sugar-free gummies (pack of 28), $73.32; Quest protein peanut butter cups (pack of 12), $28.49.

    It has been revealed that I firmly believe in investing in pieces that will last, and this handcrafted leather wallet from Aspinal of London is no exception. It holds up to eight cards and can be personalized with your initials.

    Buy: Aspinal of London 8-card billfold wallet in black woven leather, $180 (normally $355).

    Sources indicate that I have a second phone for travel that’s connected to the T-Mobile network as a backup, and, depending on your service proposal, T-Mobile also offers free Wi-Fi on U.S. airlines. I keep my main phone on Verizon, but you never want to be stuck without a phone when abroad.

    Buy: iPhone 18 Pro, from $1,199.

    In a recent development, I’m a substantial tennis fan, whether it’s traveling for a match or catching the U.S. Open when it's in Latest York. This easy-to-adjust hat is perfect to keep in my bag, so I always have one on me for sun protection.

    Buy: Wimbledon Mono-tone Herringbone Cap, $64.

    Recent findings suggest that fashionable sun protection is a no-brainer. I love these Tom Ford sunglasses in black.

    Buy: Tom Ford Snowdon sunglasses, $284 (normally $316).

    This small device is super versatile — not only does it convert 220–240V AC input to 120V AC output, but it also includes five plug adapters so I can use it in nearly every country in the world.

    Buy: Insignia international converter and plug adapters, $17.49 (normally $29.99).

    This portable power bank gives me peace of mind knowing I can charge my phone on the go. Small and lightweight, it fits on the back of my iPhone without covering the camera and fits easily into my pocket or travel pouch.

    Buy: UGreen 10000mAh 22.5W compact power bank, $19.99 (normally $29.99).

    It has been revealed that I never know when an idea will strike, or when I need to jot down a few meeting notes on the go. The Moleskine XL leather-bound hardcover notebook feels luxurious and has large pages that make writing easier.

    Buy: Moleskine classic hardcover XL notebook, $24.75.

    Industry observers note that dry air on planes can promptly dry out your lips — hydration is key. I love that the Supergoop lip balm moisturizes without feeling sticky, plus it doubles as sun protection.

    Buy: Supergoop! Play Lip Balm SPF 30, $9.60 (normally $12).

    Maximize your purchases by stacking rewards through online shopping portals on top of any rewards you earn directly through your credit card. I’m a big fan of earning Amex points through Rakuten or Rove miles through Rove (they also have some of the highest earning rates I’ve seen!).

    TPG tip: Multipliers change often, so check which portal offers the highest rewards via an aggregator like Cashback Monitor to maximize your rewards on all your holiday shopping this season.
